Startup Product Management Entrepreneurship Web3 Software Development The Question I Ask Every Founder in the First 10 Minutes and Why Most Cannot Answer It Taher Pittalvala 8 min read · Sep 25, 2026 -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size After 150+ founder conversations the pattern is consistent. The ones who answer this clearly build faster, waste less, and ship something real users actually want. Every founder I work with has a product idea. Most have thought about it for months. Some have a pitch deck. Some have a prototype. A few have already spoken to development companies and received quotes. Almost none of them can answer the first question I ask. The question is not about technology. It is not about budget or timeline or features. It is the question that determines whether everything else we discuss in that conversation is worth discussing at all. Who specifically will use this product on day one, and what specific problem does it solve for that specific person? Not a market. Not a demographic. Not a country or a continent or a global audience. A specific person, doing a specific thing, with a specific frustration that the product addresses better than whatever they are doing today. Most founders cannot answer it. Not because they have not thought about their audience. Because the way they have thought about their audience is too broad to be useful. What Founders Actually Say When I ask this question, the answers fall into two categories. The first category is geography. The founder tells me which country or region they are targeting. India. The UAE. The UK. Or, most commonly, global. Global is not an audience. Global is the absence of an audience definition. A product that is for everyone is designed for no one in particular, which means the user experience, the onboarding, the payment options, the language, the trust signals, and the support model are all being designed around an imaginary average user who does not actually exist anywhere. The second category is industry or category. The founder tells me they are targeting small businesses, or real estate professionals, or healthcare workers, or students. This is better than geography but still not specific enough to make product decisions from. Small businesses in which country? With what size team? At what stage of their growth? Using what existing tools? With what budget for new software? With what level of technical sophistication? Every one of these variables changes the product significantly. A small business in the UAE has different payment preferences, different regulatory requirements, different communication habits, and different software expectations than a small business in Germany or Nigeria or the Philippines, even if they are in the same industry. The founders who build successful products are not the ones who defined the largest possible audience at the start. They are the ones who got brutally specific about one type of person in one context with one problem and then expanded from there once they had proven the core product worked. The Geography Problem Nobody Talks About Press enter or click to view image in full size Knowing who your user is does not automatically tell you how they behave in their specific geography. These three gaps are the ones that most consistently damage conversion after launch. Even founders who know their audience reasonably well often miss the second layer of the question. Knowing who your user is does not automatically tell you how they behave in their specific geography, and user behaviour varies significantly across markets in ways that are not obvious until you are already building. Language is the most visible example but often the least well thought through. A founder building a product for a global audience assumes English because English is the language of the internet and the startup world. What they miss is that English may not be the first language or the preference of their target user, even if that user speaks it fluently. A user who reads and processes information primarily in Arabic, Hindi, or Mandarin is a different design problem than a user who reads primarily in English. The direction of text, the length of words, the cultural references in error messages and onboarding copy, the trust signals that feel familiar versus foreign all of these affect whether a user who speaks English well enough to use the product actually feels comfortable enough to trust it with their money or their data. Payment is the second and often more immediately damaging blind spot. A founder building a SaaS product assumes card payments because that is how software is purchased in the US and UK. They discover after launch that a significant portion of their target audience in their target geography does not use cards for online transactions, or does not trust card payments for international platforms, or has a strong preference for a local payment method that the product does not support. Cash on delivery, bank transfers, mobile money, buy-now-pay-later models, and local digital wallets are the primary payment methods for large portions of the world’s internet users. A product that only accepts Visa and Mastercard is not accessible to a significant share of its potential market, and the founder often does not discover this until they are wondering why traffic is not converting.
